transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~44 minutes
Attendees: Mark Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Julian Park (StellarCart Eng Lead), Rosa Alvarez (StellarCart PM), Amir Khan (StellarCart SRE)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, core params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retry/backoff patterns. Also demoed Console traces and an Optimize suggestion for batching/cache. Customer wants clarity on latency SLOs and impact on token cost; ask for benchmark sheet and POC scope.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API streaming semantics and chunk behavior
- Parameter effects and defaults (temp, top_p, stop sequences, max tokens)
- Retries, idempotency and backoff recommendations
- Console observability: per-request trace, token cost breakdown
- Optimize recommendations: batching, KV prefix cache, quantization recs for Dedicated
- Security & compliance asks (SOC2, data retention)

Transcript:
[00:00:12] Mark (AE): hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, we'll do a quick 40 minute run through of the hosted chat path and then show the console traces and one Optimize suggestion. Priya is going to demo the streaming bits.
[00:00:25] Rosa (Customer): thanks, Mark, excited — we're mostly here because we want a predictable latency profile for live chat in checkout flows. 150ms p95 would be ideal but we'll take higher if cost is better.
[00:00:37] Priya (SE): great, thanks Rosa. quick note: hosted streaming sends small delta events as tokens become available — you'll see chunk sizes typically every 50-150ms depending on batch and model. in practice p50 is often sub 100ms but p95 is where you tune.
[00:00:51] Julian (Customer): can you explain how params change that? like, temperature and stuff?
[00:00:56] Priya (SE): absolutely. temperature mostly affects randomness not latency. top_p similarly affects distribution but again small effect on runtime. the big latency drivers are sequence length (prompt + generated tokens), model choice, and batching. so if you set max_tokens high you obviously increase tail latency for longer generations.
[00:01:20] Amir (SRE): when you say batching, are you batching on the Redwood side? do we control that?
[00:01:26] Priya (SE): yes — the runtime performs continuous batching. you can tune the concurrency from the client side (parallel requests) and on the server side we have autoscale + batch windows. Redwood Optimize will suggest a batching profile based on observed QPS to hit your SLOs while minimizing per-token cost. note: for very low latency SLOs we recommend smaller batch windows or pinning to Dedicated pools.
[00:01:49] Mark (AE): also want to flag tradeoffs — Dedicated (reserved capacity) gives steadier latency and better cost at scale, hosted is fastest to start.
[00:01:58] Rosa: we might start hosted during experiment then move to Dedicated in prod. what's the fallback story if a hosted model is overloaded?
[00:02:06] Priya: good question. smart routing rules will failover to compatible model variants automatically — you can define policies: cost-first or latency-first. there's also an automatic degraded mode where we reduce max_tokens or serve cached prefix responses. sometimes transcript shows "K-V cash" in auto notes but that's the KV cache.
[00:02:26] Julian: curious about retries — if we hit a 500 or get a stalled stream, what's the recommended client behavior?
[00:02:32] Priya: client should use idempotency keys for non-streaming generation calls. for streaming we recommend an exponential backoff with jitter: start at 200ms, 2x, up to ~2s and rehydrate the prefix cache so you don't re-generate the same tokens. for short-lived problems a quick retry is fine. we demoed a retry helper in the SDK.
[00:02:52] Mark: and corner case — partial stream losses. if you lose the last chunk, best practice is to ask the model to continue from last known token with a small overlap; we add a small overlap window to avoid duplication.
[00:03:06] Rosa: okay. can you show the console so we can see a live request trace and cost breakdown?
[00:03:12] Priya: yeah, switching to console now — 1 sec — sharing screen — this is the request detail: duration, token counts, per-token cost, and model used. you can see a streaming trace with time slices.
[00:03:32] [screen-share noise, brief crosstalk]
[00:03:40] Priya: here's a sample trace — prompt was ~280 tokens, generated 120 tokens. the console shows that the first 50 tokens came in quick succession then a small pause — that's normal because of batching window. under traces we also surface queue time and kernel selection.
[00:03:58] Julian: that queue time number — is that client queuing or server?
[00:04:02] Priya: server-side queue time; it shows how long request waited to be batched. if this rises you either need more reserved capacity or tweak batch windows. Optimize will recommend those changes.
[00:04:12] Amir: any data retention concerns? what about logs that contain user PII?
[00:04:18] Mark: we offer configurable retention and encryption at rest. for hosted we have a default retention window (30 days) and an enterprise option for shorter retention and no-capture mode. we can discuss SOC2 scope — we'll share the security pack.
[00:04:30] Rosa: great — we'll need that security doc.
[00:04:33] Priya: back to streaming — a practical tip: if you have predictable prompt prefixes (like a system prompt + user history) use prefix caching — it reduces latency and token cost massively because KV cache avoids redoing early layers. we'll test that during the POC.
[00:04:49] Julian: how much of a reduction are we talking about?
[00:04:52] Priya: ranges — often 20-60% token reduction on repeated prefixes. for chatty flows with the same system prompt every call it's significant. depends on prompt variability.
[00:04:59] Mark: i'll note that in the benchmark sheet.
[00:05:03] Rosa: can you demo parameter tuning quickly — say we tune temperature from 0.2 to 0.8 how does that show in the console?
[00:05:10] Priya: yep — running a quick demo. sending two parallel calls with identical prompts and different temps — watch the streams. you'll see the outputs diverge; the latency is nearly identical. console shows token cost the same, same model, so cost delta negligible. temp affects quality not cost.
[00:05:32] [typing sounds; short pause]
[00:05:42] Priya: one more advanced point — top_p vs temperature interplay; often we keep temp low and use top_p to control creativity. but none of these affect kernel choice unless you change model size.
[00:05:56] Julian: what about stop sequences and truncation? sometimes we get incomplete json from the model in our structured outputs.
[00:06:02] Priya: for structured outputs use function/tool calling or the structured schema feature; if you must parse streaming tokens, include strong stop tokens and validate on the client. also the console has a structured-output monitor that flags partial JSONs as a quality regression.
[00:06:16] Rosa: show us the Optimize suggestion you mentioned earlier.
[00:06:20] Priya: switching panels — Optimize flagged three things for this sample workload: 1) enable prefix cache on repeated system prompts, 2) reduce batch window to 10ms for the low-latency route, 3) suggest a mixed model strategy — smaller model for short generative replies, larger for long-form.
[00:06:38] Mark: note that mixed model routing can be automated — request routed by policy (latency-first or cost-first), we fall back if capacity is constrained.
[00:06:46] Amir: any guidance for tokenization weirdness — we saw off-by-one tokens causing prompt length surprises.
[00:06:52] Priya: token counters in the console use the model's tokenizer; when you construct prompts consider normalizing whitespace and beware of invisible unicode. we also expose tokenization API to pre-count.
[00:07:05] Julian: about retries again — what's the SDK doing to avoid double billing?
[00:07:09] Priya: idempotency keys for sync calls. when streaming you can't fully de-duplicate mid-stream but we recommend policies: record last successful token index and resume from overlap. billing is per final accepted generation; transient retries that are aborted are not charged beyond compute used but we can share exact billing semantics in doc.
[00:07:28] Rosa: will need that clarification for finance.
[00:07:31] Mark: sure — will include pricing examples in the follow-up.
[00:07:34] [small laugh]
[00:07:38] Priya: also run a quick failover example — i'm going to throttle one request to trigger fallback to a cheaper variant. you'll see the console label it as fallback and show policy reason.
[00:07:50] [demo noise, shared screen]
[00:08:05] Priya: fallback engaged — note the minor quality delta and a 30% cost saving in this synthetic case.
[00:08:12] Julian: acceptable if we can detect it and maybe surface to users as "low-fidelity answer"?
[00:08:17] Mark: yep — you can add metadata tags on responses so product can display a banner or reroute to a higher-quality variant on demand.
[00:08:25] Rosa: staffing question — for the POC who will do the infra checks?
[00:08:29] Mark: Priya and I will coordinate; for Dedicated you'll also want Infra involvement. we'll set a call with your infra and security folks.
[00:08:36] Amir: timeline — we're hoping for a 4-week POC followed by a pilot.
[00:08:40] Priya: that sounds doable; POC checklist: sample workload, QPS target, latency SLOs, security contact, and test data. we'll run small benchmarks first.
[00:08:49] Rosa: can you capture the conversation about the console trace and append it to the ticket?
[00:08:53] Mark: yes — i'll upload the recording and the trace export.
[00:08:58] [brief pause]
[00:09:05] Priya: quick note about private deployments — if you need VPC or on-prem we have a private control plane and can map the same APIs. there are extra lead times but same interface. some customers prefer private for PII-sensitive flows.
[00:09:20] Julian: okay, we'll decide after POC.
[00:09:24] Rosa: anything about monitoring? we'd like alerts for p95 latency drift and sudden token spike anomalies.
[00:09:30] Priya: console supports alerting on per-route latency and token usage. Optimize also has anomaly detection we can wire up to Slack or PagerDuty.
[00:09:38] Mark: action items and next steps we'll summarize at the end.
[00:09:42] [discussion of small UI tweaks and screen flicker]
[00:10:05] Priya: one last pro tip — for mobile clients try early-token streaming: send first few tokens asap to client to improve perceived latency even if backend is still generating. Combine with small initial syntactic tokens to get quick DOM updates.
[00:10:25] Julian: nice.
[00:10:28] Rosa: ok let's do the recap?
[00:10:30] Mark: recap: 1) we'll send benchmark sheet and security pack; 2) Priya will run prefix cache A/B and model latency test; 3) set POC: 4 weeks, objectives: reach 150-300ms p95 in a staged path and measure cost per active session.
[00:10:47] Julian: agreed.
[00:10:49] Amir: agreed.
[00:10:50] Rosa: thanks Mark, Priya. good demo.
[00:10:55] Mark: thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the POC kickoff next week.
[00:11:03] [meeting closes, recording stops]
